Methods

Algorithm and implementation details

Source: vignettes/methods.qmd

Overview

rePredRet predicts retention times by directly mapping between chromatographic systems using monotonically constrained Generalized Additive Models (GAMs). This approach is based on the observation that elution order is largely conserved between similar chromatographic systems.

Algorithm

Core Principle

If compound A elutes before compound B in chromatographic system 1, it will likely also elute before B in a similar system 2. This relationship can be modeled as a monotonic function:

RTtarget=f(RTsource)RT_{target} = f(RT_{source})

where ff is a monotonically increasing function.

Model Fitting

  1. Identify Common Compounds: Find compounds present in both source and target systems using standardized InChI identifiers (with stereochemistry stripped for better matching).

  2. Fit Monotonic GAM (using mgcv):

    • If there are fewer than 4 distinct source RTs, they are jittered by up to 0.01 with a fixed seed, so the same data always give the same model
    • An unconstrained thin plate regression spline GAM gives the smoothing parameter
    • Compounds with large residuals are down-weighted with a sigmoid weight (0.5 at a residual of 10% of the maximum target RT, steepness 30). These two values were set by eye for the original PredRet and have never been optimized
    • A cubic regression spline is refitted with monotonic increasing constraints (mgcv::mono.con() and mgcv::pcls())

  3. Prediction Intervals: three methods share the fit above. See the benchmark article for their coverage and speed.

    method = "adaptive_pi" (default): the width of the interval follows the local scatter of the calibration compounds, and its level is calibrated by cross-validated conformal prediction.

    • Cross-validated residuals: the compounds are split into 5 folds, interleaved along the source RT. Each fold is predicted by the monotone spline refitted on the other folds (with the smoothing parameter and weights of the full fit). These residuals include the uncertainty of the fitted curve.
    • Local scale s(x): a Gamma GAM (log link, REML, at most 5 basis functions) of the absolute residuals, weighted by the sigmoid outlier weights so that a single outlier does not widen the band around it. s(x) is floored at 30% of the global scale.
    • Calibration: the multiplier q is the conformal quantile of the normalized residuals |e| / s(x): the ⌈(n + 1) · 0.95⌉-th smallest. With fewer than 19 compounds this is the largest one.
    • Interval: fit ± q · s(x). Each bound is made non-decreasing by isotonic regression, which keeps lower ≤ fit ≤ upper, and the lower bound is truncated at 0.

    method = "fast_ci": about 4 times faster, with an interval of nearly constant width.

    • fit ± z · sqrt(SE² + σ²), where SE is the pointwise standard error of the unconstrained GAM and σ² the mean squared leave-one-out residual (the constrained fit’s residuals divided by 1 − leverage)
    • Bounds are made monotone and truncated at 0 as above

    method = "bootstrap": about 40 times slower than adaptive_pi.

    • The monotone fit is repeated on 200 bootstrap resamples. Each compound is predicted by the refits whose resample did not include it (out-of-bag), which gives out-of-sample residuals
    • These residuals go through the same local scale and conformal calibration as adaptive_pi (jackknife+-after-bootstrap)

    On held-out compounds from 135 RepoRT system pairs the 95% intervals covered 94.6% (adaptive_pi), 95.5% (fast_ci) and 94.8% (bootstrap) of the compounds. In the regions with the least / most scatter adaptive_pi covered 94.8% / 94.5%, while fast_ci covered 97.4% / 93.4%: a constant width is too wide where compounds agree and too narrow where they scatter.

    Few compounds: with only 10–15 shared compounds no method reaches the nominal level. Coverage was 86% (adaptive_pi), 90% (fast_ci) and 89% (bootstrap). With so few compounds, a 95% interval would have to be very wide to hold. Treat intervals from models with fewer than about 20 compounds as roughly 85–90% intervals.

  4. Quality Filters: Predictions are only made where:

    • CI width < 2 minutes OR relative CI width < 20%
    • Source RT is in a dense region of calibration data (density check)

GAM Specification 

# Unconstrained fit for the smoothing parameter
fit <- mgcv::gam(y ~ s(x, k = k, bs = "tp"), data = calibration_data)

# Monotonic constrained refit
sm <- mgcv::smoothCon(mgcv::s(x, k = k, bs = "cr"), calibration_data)[[1]]
con <- mgcv::mono.con(sm$xp)
p <- mgcv::pcls(list(X = sm$X, y = y, w = w, sp = fit$sp, S = sm$S,
                     Ain = con$A, bin = con$b, p = sm$xp, C = matrix(0, 0, 0), off = 0))
  • k: number of unique source RTs, at most 10
  • w: sigmoid weights from the unconstrained residuals

Data Source

RepoRT Repository

Retention time data comes from RepoRT (Kretschmer et al. 2024), a comprehensive repository containing:

  • Multiple chromatographic method types (RP, HILIC, etc.)
  • Standardized compound identifiers (InChI, InChIKey, SMILES)
  • Rich metadata for each chromatographic system

Compound Matching

Compounds are matched between systems using standardized InChI:

  1. Strip stereochemistry layers (/t, /b, /m, /s) from InChI
  2. Match on the remaining structural connectivity
  3. For duplicate measurements, use median RT value

Implementation

R Package Structure 

rePredRet/
├── R/
│   ├── data_loading.R           # RepoRT data loading
│   ├── gam_fitting.R            # Monotone GAM fit and bootstrap intervals
│   ├── gam_adaptive_pi.R        # Default (locally adaptive) prediction intervals
│   ├── gam_fast_ci.R            # Faster prediction intervals of nearly constant width
│   ├── model_building.R         # Model construction
│   ├── build_all_models_furrr.R # Incremental parallel pipeline
│   ├── build_user_models.R      # Models from user RT data
│   ├── prediction.R             # RT predictions
│   ├── statistics.R             # Performance metrics
│   └── user_functions.R         # Access to pre-built models
├── inst/scripts/run_pipeline.R  # Pipeline used by CI
├── tests/
│   └── testthat/                # Unit tests
└── vignettes/                   # This documentation

Key Functions

Function Purpose
download_report() Download RepoRT data
load_report_data() Load datasets from RepoRT
get_common_compounds() Find shared compounds
build_model() Build single pairwise model
build_all_models_furrr() Build all pairwise models (incremental, parallel)
predict_rt() Predict RT for a compound
generate_all_predictions() Generate all predictions

Computational Considerations

  • Parallel Processing: Models are built in parallel with furrr, one worker per available CPU core
  • Incremental Builds: Only models whose datasets changed are rebuilt
  • Model Pruning: Boot objects are pruned to reduce storage by ~95%

Validation

Cross-Validation

Model quality is assessed using leave-one-out style evaluation at calibration points:

  • R²: Coefficient of determination for predicted vs actual RT
  • Absolute Error: |predicted - actual| in minutes
  • Relative Error: |predicted - actual| / actual × 100%
  • CI Coverage: Proportion of actual values within CI

Expected Performance

Based on the original PredRet paper (Stanstrup et al. 2015):

Metric Expected Range
R² > 0.99
Median Absolute Error 0.01 - 0.28 min
Median Relative Error 1.8 - 3.7%
Median CI Width 0.08 - 1.86 min

References

  1. PredRet Algorithm: Stanstrup, J., Neumann, S., & Ivanova, I. V. (2015). PredRet: Prediction of Retention Time by Direct Mapping between Multiple Chromatographic Systems. Analytical Chemistry, 87(18), 9421-9428. doi:10.1021/acs.analchem.5b02287

  2. RepoRT Database: Kretschmer, F., Witting, M., & al. (2024). RepoRT: a comprehensive repository for small molecule retention times. Nature Methods, 21, 153-155. doi:10.1038/s41592-023-02143-z

  3. Generalized Additive Models: Wood, S. N. (2017). Generalized Additive Models: An Introduction with R (2nd ed.). Chapman and Hall/CRC.

  4. Conformal Prediction Intervals: Lei, J., G’Sell, M., Rinaldo, A., Tibshirani, R. J., & Wasserman, L. (2018). Distribution-free predictive inference for regression. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 113(523), 1094-1111.
